summary: This informational memo describes the Data Link Switching Client Access Protocol, used between workstations and routers to carry SNA and NetBIOS traffic over TCP sessions. It replaced RFC 2106.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2114 defines DCAP, the protocol a workstation uses to reach a DLSw router. Instead of every PC opening its own peer session to the central router, the PCs become clients of one server, which keeps a single connection to the central router on their behalf. The protocol carries SNA and NetBIOS traffic in small frames with a four-byte header over TCP, with optional multicast for finding destinations.

questions: data link switching client access protocol
how does dcap assign a mac address
subtitle: How workstations talk to a DLSw router as clients, so SNA and NetBIOS traffic can ride over TCP without one peer session per PC.

tldr.problem: DLSw is a switch-to-switch protocol, so running it on every workstation meant one TCP session per workstation to the central router, which does not scale and wastes router capacity.
tldr.mechanism: DCAP makes the workstations clients of a DCAP server rather than peers of the router. The server holds one peer connection to the central router, assigns each client a MAC address when it has none, and exchanges small fixed-header frames with them over TCP.
tldr.outcome: The central router sees one peer instead of one per workstation, and the frames reuse the DLSw state machine, so the existing DLSw behaviour is kept while the client access path becomes simpler.

facts.label: Reserved multicast addresses
facts.value: 224.0.1.49 for the server, 224.0.1.50 for the client

today: RFC 2114 is an Informational memo published in February 1997, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It revises RFC 2106 with the same protocol, and refers to RFC 1795 for the details of the DLSw switch-to-switch protocol that DCAP reuses.

sections.title: Why DCAP Exists
sections.content:
Since the Data Link Switching Protocol, RFC 1795, was published, some software vendors began implementing DLSw on workstations. The implementation of DLSw on a large number of workstations raises several important issues. Scalability is the major concern: the number of TCP sessions to the DLSw router increases in direct proportion to the number of workstations added. Efficiency is the other concern, because DLSw is a switch-to-switch protocol and is not efficient when implemented on workstations.

DCAP addresses both problems. It introduces a hierarchical structure that resolves the scalability problem, and makes all workstations clients to the router, which acts as the server, rather than peers of it. That creates a client/server model, and it provides a more efficient protocol between the workstation and the router.
sections.plainLanguage: DLSw was designed for routers talking to routers. Putting it on every PC in a school or office means one TCP connection per PC to the central router, which does not scale. DCAP turns the relationship around: the PCs become clients of one server, and the server keeps a single peer connection to the central router.

sections.title: The Client/Server Model
sections.content:
Figure 2-1 of the memo shows a typical DLSw implementation on a workstation: the workstations are connected to the central site DLSw router over the IP network, and as the network grows, scalability becomes an issue because the number of TCP sessions increases with the growing number of workstations.

Figure 2-2 shows the DCAP arrangement. The workstations are DCAP clients, attached to a DCAP server, and the DCAP server has a single peer connection to the central site router. In a large network this significantly reduces the number of peers that connect to the central site router, because the workstations and the router behave in a client/server relationship rather than as equals.
sections.plainLanguage: A DCAP server acts as a front door for the workstations. Each PC opens one connection to it, and the server opens one connection to the central router on their behalf, so the central router sees one peer instead of hundreds.

sections.title: Dynamic Address Resolution
sections.content:
In a DLSw network each workstation needs a MAC address to communicate with a front-end processor, or FEP, attached to a LAN. When DLSw is implemented on a workstation, it does not always have a MAC address defined. A workstation that connects to a router through a modem using PPP, for example, has only an IP address, and the user must then define a virtual MAC address. That is administratively intensive, since each workstation must have a unique MAC address.

DCAP uses the dynamic address resolution protocol to solve this: it permits the server to assign a MAC address to a client without complex configuration. For a client to start a session, the workstation sends a direct request to the server carrying the destination MAC address and the destination SAP. The workstation can either specify its own MAC address or ask the server to assign one to it. The server's IP address must be pre-configured on the workstation, and if IP addresses are configured for multiple servers the request can be sent to all of them, with the first one to respond being used. For a server to start a session to a client, the server sends a directed request to the workstation, and the workstation must have pre-registered its MAC address at the server, either by configuration on the server or by registration at the server, in which case both MAC and IP addresses are registered.
sections.plainLanguage: A PC on a dial-up line has no MAC address of its own, and giving every PC one by hand is a chore. With DCAP the client can simply ask the server to assign one, and the server checks that it is not already in use before handing it over.

sections.title: The Transport: TCP and Optional Multicast
sections.content:
The transport used between the client and the server is TCP, and a TCP session must be established before a frame can be sent. The default parameters are AF_INET for the socket family, SOCK_STREAM for the socket type, and port number 1973. There is only one TCP connection between a client and the server, and it is used for both read and write operations. A race condition occurs when both client and server try to establish the TCP session at the same time: the session of the initiator with the lower IP address is used and the other is closed.

Multicast and unicast with UDP support are optional. Two multicast addresses are reserved for DCAP: the server should listen for 224.0.1.49 and the client should listen for 224.0.1.50. Not all frames can travel that way. The DATA_FRAME can be sent by multicast or unicast, the CAN_U_REACH frame can be sent by multicast only, the I_CAN_REACH frame by unicast only, and all other frames only over the TCP session.

With multicast and unicast support implemented, the client does not have to configure the server's IP address. Instead of opening a TCP session to a pre-configured server, the client multicasts the CAN_U_REACH frame to the 224.0.1.49 group address. A server that can reach the destination answers with an I_CAN_REACH frame by unicast, and the client then opens the TCP connection and establishes the DCAP session. If several servers answer, the first one to reply is used. For NetBIOS traffic, NAME_QUERY and ADD_NAME_QUERY can be carried in the DATA_FRAME and sent by multicast, while NAME_RECOGNIZED and ADD_NAME_RESPONSE are carried in the DATA_FRAME and sent by unicast.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server talk over one TCP connection on port 1973. With the optional UDP support, a client can also shout a question to every server at once on a reserved multicast address and let whichever server can reach the destination answer.

sections.title: The DCAP Frame and Its Header
sections.content:
A DCAP frame has three parts: the DCAP header, the DCAP data and the user data. The protocol itself is contained in the header, which is common to all frames passed between the client and the server and is 4 bytes long. The DCAP data carries what the frame type needs in order to be processed; its structure and size depend on the message and it is optional. The user data is what the local system sends to the remote system; its size is variable and it is included only when there is data to send.

The header identifies the message type and the length of the frame. Its first byte carries the Protocol ID in the first 4 bits, set to 1000, and the Version Number in the next 4 bits, set to 0001. The second byte is the Message Type. The third and fourth bytes give the total packet length, which covers the header, the DCAP data and the user data; the minimum size of the packet is 4, the length of the header. The DCAP data for a given frame type follows the header, and the memo notes that the sender should set the reserved fields to zero while the receiver ignores them.
sections.plainLanguage: Every frame starts with the same four bytes: which protocol and version this is, what kind of frame it is, and how long the whole thing is. After that come the fields the frame type needs, and then the payload the local system wants delivered.

sections.title: The Frame Types and How a Session Runs
sections.content:
Most DCAP frames are based on the existing DLSw frames, with corresponding frames having similar names, and the functionalities are the same, so the DLSw state machine is used to handle them. Some new DCAP frames were created to handle special DCAP functions: I_CANNOT_REACH and START_DL_FAILED provide a negative acknowledgment. The DLSw frames not needed for DCAP are dropped. The memo lists the available frame types with their codes, from CAN_U_REACH at 0x01 to PEER_TEST_RSP at 0x1E.

Three exchanges matter most. A CAN_U_REACH frame is sent to the server to determine whether a resource is reachable; the server sends out an LLC explorer frame to locate the destination, and answers the client with I_CAN_REACH if the destination is reachable. If no positive acknowledgment arrives within a recommended threshold of 5 seconds the server looks again, and if there is still no response after 5 explorers the destination is considered not reachable and I_CANNOT_REACH is sent back. START_DL then asks the server to set up a circuit, and the server answers with DL_STARTED, or with START_DL_FAILED after a recommended 5 seconds and 5 attempts. HALT_DL asks to tear a session down and is answered with DL_HALTED.

Every client and server exchange capabilities as soon as the TCP session is established, and the exchange must be completed before any other frame type can be sent. CAP_XCHANGE carries the client's MAC address, or zeros if the client has none. The server checks that the address is unique, assigns one if the client has none, and returns it; the client records the address it is given, or asks for another by sending the MAC address field as zero. The flags in the frame say whether the client wants NetBIOS traffic, whether the server should keep the client's MAC and IP addresses after the TCP session goes down so it can connect back, and whether the frame is a command or a response.
sections.plainLanguage: A session runs in a fixed order. The two ends swap capabilities and agree on the client's address, the client asks whether the station it wants to reach is there, it asks for the circuit to be set up, traffic flows, and either end can ask for the circuit to be torn down.

fields.name: Protocol ID
fields.desc: The first 4 bits of byte 0, set to 1000.

fields.name: Version Number
fields.desc: The next 4 bits of byte 0, set to 0001.

fields.name: Packet Length
fields.desc: Length of the packet including header, DCAP data and user data. The minimum is 4.
